newsitem.title: UK: Funds want better corporate governance - Mobius.
newsitem.headline: Funds want better corporate governance - Mobius.

text.p: Global investors, particularly pension funds, are increasingly demanding the same high level of corporate governance in emerging markets as they expect in developed markets, investment guru Mark Mobius said.

In an interview in London, Mobius, who controls over $10 billion in 34 emerging market funds, said such investor demands would speed up the developing infrastructure of fledgling markets and bring them into the global economy more quickly.

"We are going to hear much more on this subject in coming years as the big pension funds get more exposed to emerging markets," said Mobius. "They are going to start asking questions they have not asked until now, on supervision and minority shareholders, for example."

Good corporate governance in developed markets includes everything from companies and funds focusing on shareholder value and adopting transparent and accountable management styles to avoiding conflicts of interest.
Global equity funds have been gradually increasing their weightings in more risky emerging markets over the last 10 years to achieve global diversification and higher returns.
And pension funds in developed countries, facing increasing liabilities with ageing populations and fewer contributors, are beginning to dip into emerging markets to boost returns.
But because of their more vulnerable client base, pension fund trustees often lay down much more stringent investment criteria or guidelines than those for general institutional or retail products.
Mobius said Templeton itself was becoming more demanding.

"We are much more active in this area, paying attention to company statements, going to meetings," he said. "For example, with the Hungarian retailer Fotex we were concerned about the actions of the chairman and his private companies."

Templeton said it adopted a non-confrontational but firm style with the companies they held, first approaching management to ask for an explanation, then going to local or international regulatory authorities and finally considering legal action.
Shareholder value improved after the management of Turkey's Cukurova Elektrik was approached, Mobius added, but Brazil's banking and petrochemical group Mesbla could improve disclosure.

"It used to be the case that institutional investors did not want the press exposure because it may have made them look bad, and the problem was in the price anyway -- the fund manager will just sell up and keep quiet," he said.
"But Templeton doesn't agree with that. We want to correct the situation so that the next time round it doesn't occur, and after all, we are in these markets for the long haul."

Asked if companies and authorities in emerging markets might not feel that big global investors were abusing their power, Mobius said that in fact portfolio investors had minimal influence on policies. "Foreign investors are not that powerful but you can have an impact in certain administrative areas through the judicious use of publicity."
The fund manager's last resort is to quit a market or stand back from an issue, despite a range of financial incentives on offer, if the corporate governance criteria are not met.
"We have done that for example in Indonesia where we turned down an offer because we didn't like the terms and the investing environment," Mobius said.
